newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's high unemployment masks improved job market.
newsitem.headline: Canada's high unemployment masks improved job market.

text.p: Canada's stubbornly high unemployment rate hardly budged in May according to new data on Friday, but economists said the numbers behind the headline suggested an improving job situation.
Canada's jobless rate slipped slightly to 9.5 percent in May from 9.6 percent in April -- almost twice the U.S. unemploment rate of 4.8 percent in May.
Even so, the government statistics agency, Statistics Canada, said job creation was stronger than expected, with 61,300 new jobs in May and full-time employment up by 70,300.
"Economists and labor market analysts will focus on the fact that over 60,000 jobs were created during the month," said senior economist David Rosenberg at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.

"The fact that you're seeing substantial new entry into the labor market, it's a tell-tale sign that consumer confidence is reviving," he added. "The employment gains are just barely absorbing the new entrants into the labor market, but give it time," he said.
The picture was not so rosy for young and part-time workers, with part-time jobs falling by 9,000 in May.
The unemployment rate among people aged 15 to 24 was 17.2 percent in May, up 0.2 percentage points from April and up 1.7 points from a year ago, Statistics Canada said.

Unemployment dropped significantly in Ontario -- Canada's richest and most populous province -- to 8.5 percent from 9.0 percent. In Newfoundland, the poorest province, unemployment jumped 1.4 percentage points to 20.5 percent.
The jobless rate in Canada has hovered between 9 and 10 percent since mid-1994, although the total number of jobs in the country has risen steadily over that time.

Economists said accelerating job creation had made little dent in Canada's unemployment rate partly because a large number of the unemployed had given up looking for jobs and were no longer counted in the official statistics.
The participation rate, which measures how many eligible Canadians are actively working or looking for work, has fallen steadily since 1990 to 64.9 percent this May.

"In other words, the 9.5 (percent) is understating the real extent of unemployment considerably," noted labor economist Andrew Jackson at the Canadian Labor Congress in Ottawa. "If we had the same participation rate as in 1989-90, the unemployment rate now would be over 13 percent."
Canada's jobless problem will likely top the agenda when the re-elected Liberal government's new cabinet meets next week.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals won a reduced majority in Monday's election, losing seats in the Atlantic provinces, where unemployment is the highest in Canada.
